title: MA9-01848
frame:
Forum: Refugee Protection Division (first-instance tribunal).
Parties: the claimant and the Minister; names are redacted.
Decision under review: none; this is the first-instance decision.
How the layers nest here: The member of the tribunal is the author (layer 1). The claimant and the Minister make submissions to the member (layer 2). There is no earlier decision-maker unless the reasons describe a prior decision (layer 3). Testimony and documents are layer 5.

paragraphs.text: The claimant, Mr. XXXX XXXXX XXXXX, is a citizen of Haiti. He is claiming protection in Canada under section 96 and paragraphs 97(1)(a) and 97(1)(b) of the Immigration and Refugee Protection Act (IRPA).
The following is a summary of the claimant's allegations as they appear in his Personal Information Form (PIF).
The claimant was a XXXX XXXX and a member of the XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX (XXXX) [association of XXXX XXXX XXXX]. His wife operated a XXXX store.
On XXXX, 2005, they were both victims of an attempted kidnapping by unknown armed individuals when they were in their vehicle. The claimant and his wife managed to escape before being kidnapped.
On XXXX, 2009, the claimant and his colleague received threatening telephone calls from individuals telling them they were no longer welcome at XXXX.
On XXXX, 2009, the claimant's colleague was shot to death.
The claimant left Haiti on XXXX, 2009, to go to the United States. On XXXX, 2009, he went to the Canadian border and made a claim for refugee protection.

The panel is satisfied as to the claimant identity given the exhibits entered on the record,1 namely his Haitian passport, his driver's licence, his national identification card and his birth certificate.
After reviewing the documentary and testimonial evidence, the panel determines that the claimant is not a Convention refugee or a person in need of protection, for the reasons stated hereafter.

The panel is of the opinion that the claimant did not establish a well-founded fear of persecution on one of the five Convention grounds, namely - as his lawyer argued - by reason of his membership in a particular social group, specifically that of wealthy citizens and the XXXX XXXX association. The claimant's lawyer also argued that the claimant may fear persecution by reason of his imputed political opinion since he stated that the weapons used by the criminals to commit their crimes of theft and kidnapping were provided by the government. When the claimant was asked about the source of his information, he said he heard it on the radio and that, as a Haitian, he always knew that.
The panel repeatedly asked the claimant what he fears about returning to Haiti and the reasons why he fears returning there.

Invariably, the claimant responded that he feared being robbed, kidnapped and possibly killed if he were to return to Haiti. The claimant essentially fears being the victim of a crime for being perceived to have money because he travelled and he was criticized for living extravagantly. He was threatened for those reasons in XXXX 2009. He said his fellow XXXX XXXX, XXXX XXXX, had also been threatened for that reason and was criticized for buying a new car.

The panel pointed out to the claimant that in his account, in question 31 of his PIF,2 he wrote at line 38 that the threats consisted in the claimant being told he was to steer clear of the association in Port-au-Prince and elsewhere. When asked why he failed to testify about the threats he received as a member of the XXXX, the claimant said the criminals had changed their threats to include the association. Nonetheless, the claimant explained that he was threatened because there was money within the association. The claimant said the role of the association of XXXX XXXX XXXX was to XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX. In fact, he said it was a XXXX company that XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX.

Therefore, the association of which the claimant was a member would not constitute, within the meaning of Ward,3 "groups whose members voluntarily associate for reasons so fundamental to their human dignity that they should not be forced to forsake the association" or a group "associated by a former voluntary status, unalterable due to its historical permanence." It is a XXXX XXXX association that XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX. It is a commercial association. The panel determines that the claimant's fear, even though it was linked to his membership to this association, does not correspond to membership in a "particular social group" because the association is a profit-earning business association.

What is more, a group of wealthy people would not constitute a particular social group within the meaning of Ward.4 It is not a group defined by an innate, unchangeable characteristic, a group whose members voluntarily associate for reasons fundamental to their human dignity, or a group associated by a former voluntary status, unalterable due to its historical permanence.
The claimant indicated that if he were to return to Haiti, he would change jobs and open a business. It is therefore not fundamental for him to be a XXXX XXXX.

The same argument can be made for XXXX XXXX. There is no unchangeable characteristic or voluntary association for reasons related to human dignity, nor is this a group associated by a former voluntary status, unalterable due to its historical permanence.5

The claimant's counsel also argued that the claimant could fear persecution by reason of his imputed political opinion, as he stated that the weapons used by the criminals were given to them by the government as part of a vote-buying scheme. The panel fails to see how this opinion, founded or not, could make the claimant a refugee by reason of his imputed political opinion. The claimant said many times that the only reason he might be robbed, kidnapped or killed would be during a robbery such as the one committed against the claimant during the kidnapping attempt of XXXX 2005, and the profit-driven murder of his colleague in 2009. The panel determines that the claimant's prospective fear is of being a victim of crime related to the perception in Haiti that the claimant has money and not because of his real or imputed political opinion.
The claim for refugee protection cannot be analyzed under section 96 of the IRPA.

The claimant did not present evidence to the effect that he feared torture by or at the instigation of or with the consent or acquiescence of a public official or other person acting in an official capacity. The panel determines that his claim cannot be considered under paragraph 97(1)(a) of the IRPA.

The panel is of the opinion that if the claimant were to return to his country of origin, he would face a generalized risk under paragraph 97(1)(b). The panel indicated to the claimant's counsel that generalized risk is an issue for the panel.

Paragraph 97(1)(b), under which the claimant is claiming refugee protection, contains exceptions whereby the alleged fear faced by the person of being subjected to a risk to their life or a risk of cruel and unusual treatment or punishment is faced "in every part of that country and is not faced generally by other individuals in or from that country."6

The panel determines that the claimant fears common criminals who are motivated by profit. He fears them because he was a XXXX XXXX and, according to his testimony, he is perceived to have money and is therefore targeted by criminals. The panel is of the opinion that the claimant's fears stem from his association with a broad sub-group of the population, namely those perceived to have wealth in Haiti.

Although people perceived to have wealth can be at greater risk, the panel determines that a broad sub-group of the population faces this risk and that all these people in Haiti who represent a potential source of illicit gain in the eyes of criminals might be targeted. This is a generalized risk.

According to the documentation, the crime rate is extremely high in Haiti, given how destitute that country has been for the past several years and the lack of effective law enforcement. In that context, anyone perceived to have any cash is at risk of being a victim of crime.7 The issue of generalized risk is a principle confirmed by the jurisprudence in Prophète.8 Justice Tremblay-Lamer noted: "The risk of all forms of criminality is general and felt by all Haitians. While a specific number of individuals may be targeted more frequently because of their wealth, all Haitians are at risk of becoming the victims of violence." What is more, jurisprudence has confirmed a decision by the Immigration and Refugee Board, Refugee Protection Division, whereby wealthy people in Haiti do not face a higher risk than other Haitians.9 The panel determines that the risk faced by the claimant is no different than the risk faced by other members of this broad sub-group, namely those perceived to have wealth.
For these reasons, the panel determines that XXXX XXXX XXXX claim cannot be accepted under paragraph 97(1)(b) of the IRPA.
For the reasons set out above, the panel rejects XXXX XXXX XXXX claim for refugee protection and finds that he is not a Convention refugee or a person in need of protection.

His claim is rejected.
